conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been vomiting nonstop since yesterday. I can’t keep anything down — not even water. It feels just like my last gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I have a gastric pacer, so MRIs are out. My PCP said I shouldn’t have one, which was part of the plan before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important — we’ll keep that in mind. You’re not having abdominal pain, fever, or dizziness when standing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain, no fever. I feel weak, but I’m not dizzy when I stand. I did pass gas and had a bowel movement yesterday, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring — it means your bowels are moving, so we don’t suspect a blockage. We’ll start IV fluids and some anti-nausea meds right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I just need to stop vomiting. I’m so dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you Zofran, Compazine, Reglan, and Ativan through the IV. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, but still nauseous. I haven’t thrown up since I got here, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your blood pressure was high in the ER — 181 over 93 — likely from vomiting and dehydration. We gave a dose of IV metoprolol to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on lisinopril and metoprolol at home. Should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you can tolerate pills, we’ll restart your oral metoprolol. Lisinopril too, but we’ll watch your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My blood sugar’s probably high too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 327 on admission, and your urine showed ketones. We’re not sure if it’s full DKA, but we’re treating it like mild ketoacidosis with insulin and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my glargine at night and lispro as needed. Should I adjust anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your usual insulin regimen — no changes. We’ll monitor your sugars closely and adjust the sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea seems a bit better? We’re going to try a small sip of water to see if you can tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little less nauseous. I’ll try the water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great — you kept the water down. We’ll advance to ice chips and maybe clear liquids later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried I’d never be able to eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs from this morning show your kidney function is improving — creatinine down to 0.6. Your glucose is now 152, and ketones are clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the tachycardia? My heart’s been racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate was 133 in the ER — likely from dehydration and nausea. The EKG shows sinus tachycardia, no acute changes. It’s down to 95 now, so it’s improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not something serious with my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Me too. The EKG had some non-specific changes, but nothing new compared to your last one. Likely due to lead placement or body habitus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on clear liquids all afternoon and haven’t vomited. We’re going to try a soft diet — applesauce and crackers — in small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I’m hungry. I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent — you kept the soft food down. Your nausea is much improved. We’ll keep you on metoclopramide three times a day and add ondansetron as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I keep using the Compazine suppository at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send it home with you for breakthrough nausea. Also, continue pantoprazole twice daily — it helps with reflux, which can worsen gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking — my last gastric emptying study was normal. Does that mean it’s not really gastroparesis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You did have a normal study recently, but you’ve had abnormal ones in the past. Symptoms can flare even if tests are normal now. We’re treating based on your clinical picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I just want to avoid another hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs look great — glucose is 134, no ketones, and your electrolytes are stable. Hemoglobin dropped a bit, but it’s likely from dilution with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the urine test okay? I heard they did a culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the culture showed mixed bacteria, but it’s consistent with contamination — not a UTI. So no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re tolerating food, nausea is gone, and your vitals are stable. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual medications — insulin, metoprolol, lisinopril, metoclopramide, and pantoprazole. Use ondansetron or Compazine if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your PCP and endocrinologist. If nausea returns, call them early — don’t wait until you’re dehydrated again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we hope not to see you back here soon.
